source.text: Πρῶτον πάντων πίστευσον ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ Θεός, ὁ τὰ πάντα κτίσας καὶ καταρτίσας, καὶ ποιήσας ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι τὰ πάντα, καὶ πάντα χωρῶν, μόνος δὲ ἀχώρητος ὤν. 2. πίστευσον οὖν αὐτῷ καὶ φοβήθητι αὐτόν, φοβηθεὶς δὲ ἐγκράτευσαι. ταῦτα φύλασσε καὶ ἀποβαλεῖς πᾶσαν πονηρίαν ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ καὶ ἐνδύσῃ πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν δικαιοσύνης καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, ἐὰν φυλάξῃς τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην.
source.label: Mandate 1

translation.text: First of all[1], believe that God is one—the one who created and set in order all things, and brought all things into being from what was not, and who encompasses all things, while he alone is uncontainable. Therefore believe him and fear him; and having feared, practice self-control. Keep these things, and you will throw off every wickedness from yourself and put on every virtue of righteousness, and you will live to God[a][5][4][3][2], if you keep this command.

footnotes.text: Lit. "from the not-being into being"; also rendered "from non-being into being" or paraphrased "out of nothing."
Or: "contains all things, being himself uncontained."
Or: "clothe yourself with every virtue of righteousness."
Or 'and you will live for God'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic adverbial phrase introducing the primary command; "First of all" preserves priority without sounding archaic.
With a content clause (ὅτι), pisteuō naturally means to accept a proposition as true.
Both are possible; "God is one" keeps the creedal ring and mirrors the Greek structure closely.
κτίζω commonly denotes divine creation; "created" is the standard, weighty term.
καταρτίζω here complements κτίζω; "set in order" conveys arranging/ordering the created world without importing later technical nuances.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ποιήσας ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι τὰ πάντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: brought all things into being from what was not
alternatives: made all things from non-being into being
made all things out of nothing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression literally reads "from the not-being into being"; "brought ... into being from what was not" keeps the Greek structure and avoids overinterpretive phrasing while preserving the ex nihilo sense.
χωρέω can mean "to have room for, contain"; "encompasses" captures the metaphysical scope without suggesting mere physical containment or the English sense of "comprehend=understand."
From χωρέω with alpha-privative; "uncontainable" maintains the lexical parallel. "Incomprehensible" is a later theological sense that could mislead in English.
With the dative (αὐτῷ), pisteuō often has the nuance of relational trust; the shift from "believe that" to "trust him" reflects the change in construction and sense.
Preserves the strong biblical/early Christian idiom of the fear of God without euphemizing.
Aorist middle imperative of ἐγκρατεύομαι; "practice self-control" communicates the active moral discipline called for.
"Keep" is the standard rendering of φυλάσσω in moral exhortation contexts; it keeps the imperative's force crisp.
ἀποβάλλω means to throw away/off; "throw off" is vivid and retains the metaphorical texture.
In general moral contexts, "wickedness" captures the broad scope of moral evil inherent in πονηρία.
ἐνδύω in the middle voice frequently uses the clothing metaphor; "put on" is concise and transparent.
"Virtue" is the most direct English equivalent and matches early Christian moral vocabulary.
Default project rendering; in this moral context "righteousness" is the better fit for personal ethical quality.
Dative of reference/advantage; "for God" communicates orientation and purpose without the stiffness of "to God."
"Command" is plain and matches the internal diction; "mandate" is the section title but would be confusing in-line.

theological_decisions.issue: Creation ex nihilo implied by ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Rendered as "brought all things into being from what was not"
alternative_readings: "made all things out of nothing" (more interpretive)
"made all things from what did not yet exist" (softened)
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek idiom literally states "from the not-being into being." The chosen rendering preserves the structure and allows the ex nihilo implication without importing later philosophical phrasing.

theological_decisions.issue: Divine transcendence in πάντα χωρῶν, μόνος δὲ ἀχώρητος
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: "encompasses all things, while he alone is uncontainable"
theological_decisions.rationale: Maintains the lexical parallel with χωρέω/ἀχώρητος while avoiding English "comprehend" (understand) ambiguity; emphasizes God's transcendence over creation rather than cognitive unknowability.
Hermas’s paraenetic tone favors the stronger traditional idiom of fearing God as a moral restraint leading to self-control.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Fear of God in early Christian ethics

theological_decisions.rationale: The dative construction invites a relational nuance beyond mere assent; distinguishing the two imperatives (believe that / trust him) preserves Hermas’s movement from creed to reliance and obedience.
"For God" communicates orientation and purpose in contemporary English without losing the dative’s force; it avoids unintended Pauline echo while remaining faithful.

review_passes.summary: The draft is excellent. It accurately captures the theological weight, the specific vocabulary of Hermas (e.g., creation ex nihilo, the fear of God, living to/for God), and the paraenetic tone of the Mandates. The lexical choices are well-reasoned and faithful to the Greek.

translation.text: First, believe that there is one God. He created and ordered everything. He brought all things into existence from nothing. He holds all things, but nothing can hold him. So believe in him and fear him. Let that fear lead you to practice self-control. Keep these instructions, and you will throw off all wickedness and clothe yourself with every righteous virtue. You will live for God if you keep this command.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: First, believe that there is one God. He created and ordered everything. He brought all things into existence from nothing. He holds all things, but nothing can hold him. So believe in him and fear him. Let that fear lead you to practice self-control. Keep these teachings, and you will throw off all wickedness and clothe yourself with every righteous virtue. You will live for God if you keep this command.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is substantially clearer while preserving the creation-from-nothing claim, God’s transcendence, the fear/self-control sequence, and the imagery of casting off evil and putting on virtue. The causal clarification of fear leading to self-control is warranted by the immediate sequence and is appropriately identified in the audit trail. A small revision is needed because “teachings” adds a doctrinal-category nuance not present in “these things”; “instructions” communicates the imperative context more naturally without making that shift.
